PART 1: NARRATION READY
Let me walk you through what we're seeing on T10 this May. T10 is a 3,000 kVA transformer — a serious piece of equipment — and right now it is running in an untuned condition. What that means in practice is that the field is generating waste across three categories simultaneously: energy losses, thermal burden, and cooling overhead. When you add those up, we're looking at an estimated $662,250 per year in total waste from this one transformer. That number is not an anomaly — it reflects the structural character of how this field is operating day in and day out. The power factor — the efficiency ratio of how well your transformer converts delivered apparent power into real productive work — is averaging 89.7% across May. That sounds close to acceptable, but the minimum drops to 81.4% during peak production intervals. That gap between average and minimum tells you the field is swinging, and swinging fields are expensive fields. The reactive burden sits at 420.6 kVAR on average, spiking to 760.5 kVAR at its worst. That reactive draw is not doing any work — it's circulating magnetizing current through your conductors and transformer core, generating heat and consuming capacity that could be supporting productive load. The voltage picture is also a concern. Your average voltage for the month is 457.4 volts on a 480-volt system — that's a chronic 22-volt deficit. And during three distinct drop events in May, the field fell to readings in the low 430s. At 10% below nominal, your motors are compensating by drawing extra current, which pushes directly into winding stress and thermal aging. The simulation shows that MPTS correction brings power factor to 99.5% and recovers approximately 358 kVAR on average — fundamentally changing the thermal and financial profile of this transformer. Two H490 units are indicated for this application. ---

PART 2: EXECUTIVE SHORT
Here's the executive summary on T10. This transformer is running untuned and it's costing the facility an estimated $662,250 per year in combined energy waste, thermal burden, and cooling costs. Let me take you through T10 in detail, because this transformer tells a comprehensive story about what an untuned industrial field looks like when it's under sustained, multi-dimensional stress. Start with the operating context. T10 is a 3,000 kVA transformer at the Foster Farms Cherry Avenue facility in Fresno, serving a high-intensity food processing and cold storage operation. The May 2026 dataset captures a full month of production — and what it shows is a field that is working hard, carrying significant reactive and harmonic burden, and running without the electromagnetic support it needs to do that work efficiently. **The power factor problem.** Your average power factor across May is 89.7%. In isolation, that might seem adequate. But the minimum recorded is 81.4%, and the chart body annotation flags an interval minimum of 85.17%. What that spread tells me is that this field is not holding a stable, efficient electromagnetic posture — it is swinging between moderate efficiency and significant inefficiency depending on what the production floor is doing. During those 81% intervals, nearly one in five volt-amps delivered to this transformer is being consumed by reactive and harmonic losses rather than productive work. That's a meaningful drag on every operating hour. **The reactive burden.** Average reactive draw is 420.6 kVAR. Peak reactive demand hits 760.5 kVAR. To put that in context: reactive kilovolt-amperes are the portion of apparent power that magnetizes motor windings and transformer cores without performing real mechanical or thermal work. They circulate, generate heat in conductors and cores, and consume transformer capacity. At 760.5 kVAR peak, T10 is dedicating a very substantial fraction of its apparent power capability to this non-productive burden during peak intervals. **The harmonic contribution.** The M view confirms an average iTHD of 5.4% with a maximum of 10.7%. That maximum is more than double the IEEE 519 recommended limit of 5% for this class of industrial facility. Harmonics create additional eddy current losses in the transformer core — losses that show up as heat, not as useful work. They also create electromagnetic noise that degrades the performance of variable frequency drives, programmable logic controllers, and sensitive relay systems across the facility. Amperage peaks at 1,964.8 amps on this transformer. That's a heavily loaded machine carrying a harmonically polluted current waveform, and that combination is thermally punishing. **The thermal consequence.** The thermal burden for T10 in May is 472,779 BTU per hour, against a reference baseline of 388,410 BTU per hour. That's approximately 84,000 BTU per hour of excess heat above what an efficiently operating field at this load level would generate. Removing that excess heat requires 96.5 kilowatts of mechanical cooling capacity running continuously during production — at roughly $34.05 per hour. Annualized, that cooling overhead alone is approximately $298,265. That's real money being spent on refrigeration equipment and electricity just to manage heat that an MPTS-corrected field would largely not generate. **The voltage picture.** Average voltage for the month is 457.4 volts on a 480-volt nominal system — a persistent 22-volt deficit. The minimum recorded voltage is 432.6 volts, representing a 10% sag from nominal. Three distinct clusters of triangular sag events are confirmed: near May 8th, around May 17th through 18th, and near May 23rd. These are not random utility disturbances — they are operationally triggered, likely by compressor stage starts, large motor inrush, or chiller sequencing. The clustering pattern means they are predictable and recurring. At 10% below nominal, motors pull elevated current to maintain torque — which feeds directly into winding insulation degradation and accelerated bearing wear. This is an accelerating wear signature. **The MPTS correction projection.** The simulation brings power factor from 89.7% to 99.5%. Reactive average drops from 420.6 kVAR to 62.9 kVAR. Peak reactive drops from 760.5 kVAR to 144.4 kVAR. Approximately 358 kVAR average is recovered — capacity that transforms from reactive waste to productive transformer headroom. Using the sizing rule of 760.5 kVAR MAX divided by 400, rounded up, we arrive at two H490 units for T10. At planning-level estimates, that represents an installed investment of approximately $400,000, depending on engineering scope and site conditions — a figure that should be validated through a formal engineering assessment before commitment. Against an estimated $662,250 per year in total waste, the economic case for correction on T10 is among the strongest arguments for moving tuning assignment to the front of the priority queue. Without it, this field continues to drift — efficiency falls, heat burden grows, and equipment ages faster than its design intends. That's electromagnetic stewardship — and that's the Unity standard.

T10.voltage_stability_findings:
**T10 — Voltage Health | May 2026**

The voltage story on T10 is one of chronic under-pressure. The monthly average sits at 457.4 volts on a nominal 480-volt system — that's a persistent 22-volt deficit below the reference level, representing roughly a 4.7% chronic sag across all operating hours. The full swing range across the month extends from a minimum of 432.6 volts to a maximum of 485.6 volts — a spread of approximately 53 volts peak to trough. For equipment designed to run at 480 volts, that floor is a serious concern.

What makes this finding more significant than a simple average underperformance is the clustering pattern of the triangular voltage-drop events. These characteristic downward spike shapes — the hallmark of rapid voltage sag from high-inrush events — appear in at least three distinct operational clusters during May: one near the 260508 window, a second grouping around 260517 through 260518, and a third cluster near 260523. The annotation confirms specific sag readings of 435.3 volts, 435.9 volts, and 435.1 volts at those cluster locations.

The minimum recorded voltage of 432.6 volts represents approximately a 47-volt drop from nominal — right at the 10% sag threshold. That is not a benign number. At 10% below nominal, motors in this facility are drawing elevated current to maintain torque — which feeds directly into winding temperature, insulation degradation, and accelerated bearing wear. Variable frequency drives and compressor contactors are also operating outside their optimal voltage window during these events.

The clustering behavior is operationally revealing: these drops align with production schedule patterns — compressor stage starts, large motor inrush sequences, or chiller cycling — rather than random utility disturbances. That means they are predictable, recurring, and unmitigated. Device health risk assessment for T10's voltage profile: **high**. The combination of chronic sub-nominal average voltage with recurring clustered sag events represents an accelerating wear signature that warrants immediate engineering attention.

**T10 — Reactive and Harmonic Character | May 2026**

The reactive and harmonic profile on T10 confirms what the voltage data suggests: this is a field under structural electromagnetic stress, not just occasional peak loading. The reactive burden is persistent and sizeable. The average kVAR draw across May is 420.6 kVAR, with a peak reactive demand of 760.5 kVAR maximum. These are not spikes — they are the baseline operating character of this transformer's load environment.

From the M view, the amperage trace runs at a sustained high level throughout all production windows, peaking at 1,964.8 amps maximum with a monthly average of 1,052.4 amps. That current level on a 3,000 kVA transformer tells you the load is real, heavy, and thermally significant. The reactive kVAR layer sits as a consistent structural floor beneath every productive hour — it doesn't come and go with demand peaks; it is always there, always consuming transformer capacity that could otherwise be doing productive work.

The harmonic picture adds another layer of concern. The M view shows iTHD averaging 5.4% across the month, with a maximum of 10.7% iTHD recorded during peak intervals. The IEEE 519 recommended limit for this class of industrial facility is 5% total harmonic distortion. The average is sitting right at that threshold, and the peak is more than double it. Harmonics at this level heat transformers disproportionately — the additional eddy current and hysteresis losses in the core push thermal burden well above what the fundamental load alone would generate. They also stress sensitive control electronics: VFDs, PLCs, relay coils, and compressor inverter boards are all operating in a noisier electromagnetic environment than they should be.

The minimum power factor annotation of 85.17% — visible in the chart body — combined with the header minimum of 81.4% tells you that during the worst production intervals, T10 is wasting nearly one in five delivered volt-amps to reactive and harmonic losses. That's a meaningful efficiency deficit that compounds directly into the thermal burden and cooling overhead figures.

If this transformer is operating without adequate thermal margin under current untuned conditions, winding insulation life is being consumed faster than its design expects. An infrared thermography scan of the transformer enclosure, cooling fins, and primary connections is recommended.

**MPTS sizing confirmation and tuning assignment:** Two H490 units are indicated based on the 760.5 kVAR maximum. Tuning assignment should be scheduled as a priority action — every month this field remains untuned is a month of continued $662,250-per-year-rate waste accumulation, thermal burden, and drift toward deeper inefficiency.
